title: First user interview with Dana
description: Demo conversation (synthetic, for the demo account). Alex debriefs mentor Dana on the first user interview for the side-project app with a museum educator, they discuss a pivot from exhibit prototyping to visitor testing, Dana asks a calibrated question from Never Split the Difference, and they contrast user research with market research.

utterances.text: Okay, I did it. My first real user interview for the app.
Look at you! Who was it?
An educator at the natural history museum who runs the school programs. Forty minutes of coffee.
And? What did you learn?
That my idea was kind of wrong. In a good way?
The best interviews do that. Tell me.
I pitched the prototyping part. She was polite, but she didn't care.
Why not?
Museums like hers don't design exhibits, the studios do. She cares about after it opens. Are kids using it, are they confused, do they skip the panel.
And how does she find that out now?
She stands in the gallery with a clipboard and counts. By hand. Every Tuesday.
Huh. That's a real pain.
Right? So I'm thinking of pivoting. Less exhibit prototyping, more visitor testing. A simple way to see how people move through a gallery and what they ignore.
Okay, let me ask you something. What makes you sure that's the problem worth solving, and not just her problem?
Oh. Wait, you just did the thing, didn't you? The calibrated question.
Chris Voss would be proud. But answer it.
Not sure yet. She said the other educators on her team use the same clipboard. And at the studio we did that with my tide pool table.
So a handful of people and your own job. That's a start, not proof.
Fair. Should I be looking up how big the market is? How many museums there are?

That's market research, and it's a different question. Market research asks how many people might buy this and what they'd pay. User research asks what someone actually does on a Tuesday and why it's annoying.
So one is about the size of the problem, the other is about what the problem is.
Exactly. At your stage, user research matters way more. A huge market for the wrong thing is useless.
Okay. More interviews before spreadsheets.
Five more. Different museums, different roles. And don't pitch. Ask what they did the last time they tested an exhibit.
Ask about the past, not the future.
Right. People are terrible at predicting what they'd use. They're great at complaining about what they did.
Like the studio complaining about budgets. That's where this whole idea started.
And now it's a better idea because one educator said no. How does that feel?
Weirdly good. Like the foam board prototype at work. You find out what's wrong early, while it's cheap.
